statement: AboveAnchor imposes a later forbidden run-length pair (a,b), or a long run forces a short successor, or the block product Λ=3^{∑a}/2^{∑a+k} predicts drop, or the itinerary (a_i) determines the next run. False. After the known isolated-OE ban on the first (2,1), later pairs on n<2001 are broad, including (1,3), (2,1) stays, (5,5), and (8,2). 365 drops with Λ=19683/16384>1. 365 and 1517 share (2,2,2) then split. This is not PredClosure, not a Z5 family, not a length-11 census, and not a halt theorem.

The leftover odd-escape controls have maximal odd-run itineraries 365=(2,2,2,2,1), 1517=(2,2,2,1,3), 501=(2,3,2,2,2,2,1), 6187=(2,3,2,1). After the prefix (2,2,2) the next run is 2 on 365 and 1 on 1517. On odd starts n<2001 the first pair (2,1) never stays AboveAnchor (0 stays), while a later (2,1) can stay (365: 12707 to 1196). Long-to-long pairs occur (241 realizes (5,5)). This is not a run-frequency theorem, not a residue automaton, and not a halt theorem.
